description: Believes that assigning one variable to another (b = a), or passing an object as an argument, makes an independent copy of a mutable object rather than a second name for the same object
example_wrong_answer: b is its own copy of the list, so appending to b leaves a unchanged.
source: Adapted from Progmiscon (Chiodini et al., 2021), Python: AssignmentCopiesObject

description: Believes a variable stores the expression it was assigned from and is recomputed when the variables in that expression change, instead of holding the value computed at assignment time
example_wrong_answer: size was set to len(nums), so after we append to nums, size goes up to 4 as well.
source: Adapted from Progmiscon (Chiodini et al., 2021), Python: VariablesHoldExpressions

description: Believes string methods such as upper(), replace() or strip() change the original string in place, not realising strings are immutable and these methods return a new string
example_wrong_answer: After s.upper() the variable s now holds 'HI'.

description: Believes list.copy(), list(x) or slicing x[:] also copies the nested objects inside the list, so a copy of a list of lists is fully independent
example_wrong_answer: backup is a copy, so changing backup[0][0] can't affect grid.

description: Believes range(a, b) includes the end value b (or that range(n) runs from 1 to n), rather than stopping just before b
example_wrong_answer: range(1, 3) gives 1, 2 and 3, so it prints three numbers.
source: Adapted from McMining benchmark (Al-Hossami & Bunescu, 2025, arXiv:2510.08827)

description: Believes 'and' and 'or' always evaluate both operands, not knowing that evaluation stops as soon as the result is decided by the left operand
example_wrong_answer: Both sides of the 'and' are always checked, so check('b') is called and prints too.
source: Adapted from Progmiscon (Chiodini et al., 2021), Python: NoShortCircuit

description: Believes an if/elif/else chain tests every condition and runs every branch whose condition is true, as if it were a sequence of separate if statements
example_wrong_answer: x is 15, which is greater than 10 and greater than 5, so it prints both 'big' and 'medium'.
source: Adapted from Progmiscon (Chiodini et al., 2021), Python: ConditionalIsSequence

description: Believes that in a condition like x == 'red' or 'blue' the comparison applies to both sides of 'or', so it means x == 'red' or x == 'blue'
example_wrong_answer: colour is 'green', which is neither red nor blue, so 'warm' is not printed.
source: Adapted from McMining benchmark (Al-Hossami & Bunescu, 2025, arXiv:2510.08827)

description: Believes that printing a value inside a function is the same as returning it, so the caller receives whatever the function printed
example_wrong_answer: The function prints 5, so result is 5 and the last line prints 5 again.
source: Adapted from McMining benchmark (Al-Hossami & Bunescu, 2025, arXiv:2510.08827)

description: Believes a mutable default argument (such as items=[]) is created fresh on every call, not knowing it is created once when the def statement runs and shared between calls
example_wrong_answer: Each call gets a new empty list, so the second call returns just ['b'].

description: Believes that assigning to a name inside a function changes the module-level (or enclosing) variable with the same name, without needing global or nonlocal
example_wrong_answer: The function sets count to 5, so the global count is 5 afterwards.

description: Believes a closure (e.g. a lambda defined in a loop) captures the value a variable had when the function was created, rather than looking the variable up when the function is called
example_wrong_answer: Each lambda remembers its own i, so the results are 10, 20 and 30.

description: Believes tuples can be changed in place like lists, for example by assigning to an index or calling append() or sort() on them
example_wrong_answer: A tuple is just a list with round brackets, so you can sort it or append to it the same way.

description: Believes any value, including a list or a dict, can be used as a dictionary key or set element, not knowing keys must be hashable (in practice, immutable)
example_wrong_answer: You can use [3, 4] as a key just like (1, 2); both get stored in the dict.

description: Believes list.sort() returns the sorted list, not knowing it sorts in place and returns None (unlike sorted(), which returns a new list)
example_wrong_answer: result = nums.sort() gives result = [1, 2, 3].

description: Believes a generator can be iterated over several times like a list, not knowing it is exhausted after one full pass
example_wrong_answer: The second list(gen) gives [1, 2] again, because gen still holds the same values.

description: Believes calling a generator function (or creating a generator expression) runs the body and computes all the values immediately, rather than lazily, one value per request
example_wrong_answer: Calling numbers() runs the function, so 'start' is printed before 'made'.

description: Believes yield ends the function like return, so a generator function can only ever produce its first yielded value
example_wrong_answer: The function stops at the first yield, so the list is just [1].

description: Believes __init__ creates and returns the new object (like a constructor that must return self), rather than initialising an object Python has already created
example_wrong_answer: __init__ builds the object and returns it, and that returned object is what gets stored in c.
source: Adapted from Progmiscon (Chiodini et al., 2021), Python: InitCreates and InitReturnsObject

description: Believes that assigning a new object to self inside a method replaces the object the method was called on, rather than just rebinding a local name
example_wrong_answer: rename does self = Team(new_name), so a is now the 'green' team.
source: Adapted from Progmiscon (Chiodini et al., 2021), Python: SelfAssignable

description: Believes a mutable attribute defined in the class body (e.g. members = []) gets a separate copy for every instance, not knowing it is one object shared by all instances
example_wrong_answer: Each Team gets its own members list, so b.members is still empty.

description: Believes a finally block does not run when the try or except block executes a return statement
example_wrong_answer: The try block returns straight away, so 'cleanup' is never printed.

description: Believes that after an exception is caught, execution goes back to the try block and continues with the line after the one that raised
example_wrong_answer: After the except prints its message, the next line in the try still runs, so it also prints 'stored'.

description: Believes Python picks the most specific matching except clause, rather than the first clause (top to bottom) whose type matches the exception
example_wrong_answer: Dividing by zero is a ZeroDivisionError, so the ZeroDivisionError handler runs even though except Exception comes first.

description: Believes DataFrame methods such as sort_values(), dropna() or drop() change the DataFrame they are called on, not knowing they return a new object that must be assigned
example_wrong_answer: We called df.sort_values('score'), so df is now sorted by score.

description: Believes label-based slicing with .loc excludes the end label like ordinary Python slicing, when .loc includes both endpoints
example_wrong_answer: loc['a':'b'] stops before 'b', so it only contains the value for 'a'.

description: Believes missing values (NaN) count as 0 in aggregations such as mean() or sum(), not knowing pandas skips them by default
example_wrong_answer: There are four values and two of them are NaN, which count as 0, so the mean is 53 / 4.

description: Believes arithmetic and assignment between Series or columns match values by position, not knowing pandas aligns them by index label and fills unmatched labels with NaN
example_wrong_answer: s1 + s2 just adds them element by element: 11, 22 and 33.

description: Believes that in standard CPython, using several threads makes CPU-bound pure-Python code run in parallel on multiple cores and finish faster
example_wrong_answer: With four threads on a four-core machine the number crunching runs about four times faster.

description: Believes the GIL makes multithreaded Python code thread-safe, so shared updates such as counter += 1 never need a lock
example_wrong_answer: Only one thread runs at a time because of the GIL, so counter += 1 can't race and the total is always right.

description: Believes asyncio runs coroutines in parallel on separate threads or cores, rather than interleaving them on a single thread that switches only at await points
example_wrong_answer: asyncio starts each coroutine on its own thread, so it has the same race conditions as threading and also speeds up CPU work.
